page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = logx
steps.why: The familiar 1/x dx = dt substitution converts (logx)²/x dx into a plain t² dt, with no other algebra needed.
common_mistakes: Trying integration by parts, treating (logx)² and 1/x as two separate functions to integrate by parts.
Substituting t=(logx)² instead of t=logx, which does not simplify dx/x cleanly.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever 1/x sits beside ANY power of logx, t=logx (not the whole power) is the substitution to make.

steps.label: Integrate and back-substitute for the final answer
steps.why: ∫t² dt = t³/3 + c is the plain power rule, and substituting t=logx back in raises the power of the logarithm by one, from squared to cubed.
common_mistakes: Writing (logx)²/2 instead of (logx)³/3 — the power rule raises the power by 1 and divides by the NEW power.
Forgetting to substitute logx back in for t.
steps.memory_tip: Power rule: t² integrates to t³/3 — power goes UP by one, divide by the new (higher) power, not the old one.
